definition:
Scripture speaks about money and possessions constantly, and it speaks in two registers at once. Wealth is a gift of the Creator, part of a good world meant to be enjoyed, and the Bible's first rich men, Abraham and Job among them, are counted righteous. Yet wealth is also the most dangerous rival God has for the human heart, a master that promises security and takes the soul in payment. So the Bible commands work and generosity, forbids theft, fraud, and exploitation, warns against trust in riches and against greed, and teaches contentment. Jesus sharpened all of this: “You cannot serve both God and money” (Matthew 6:24). The doctrine is not that possessions are evil but that God is the owner and people are stewards, that what is held must be held with an open hand, and that the heart follows its treasure. This study concerns wealth and possessions themselves; God's defense of the poor, the widow, and the stranger has its own study (Justice, the Poor, and the Stranger).

The Old Testament's words for wealth are ordinary words. ʿOsher means riches; hon, frequent in Proverbs, means wealth or sufficiency; chayil, which can mean strength or an army, also means wealth or substance, as when Deuteronomy says God gives Israel the power to gain wealth (Deuteronomy 8:18). Genesis says Abram was ‘very heavy’ (kaved) in livestock, silver, and gold (Genesis 13:2), using the ordinary Hebrew idiom for being rich. Two words describe interest on loans: neshek, often linked with the verb for biting, and tarbit or marbit, ‘increase’ (Leviticus 25:36-37); interpreters differ on whether the two names mark different kinds of charge or are simply paired. The tithe is maʿaser, ‘a tenth’. In the New Testament ploutos is riches and chrēmata is money or property (Mark 10:23). Mamōnas, ‘mammon’, is an Aramaic word for wealth or property that the Gospels keep untranslated, and Jesus speaks of it almost as a rival lord (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:9-13). Greed is pleonexia, the craving for more (Luke 12:15; Colossians 3:5), and the love of money is philargyria (1 Timothy 6:10); an elder must be aphilargyros, ‘free of the love of money’ (1 Timothy 3:3). Contentment is autarkeia (1 Timothy 6:6), a word the Stoics used for self-sufficiency that Paul turns into sufficiency in Christ (Philippians 4:11-13). Paul calls generosity haplotēs, a single-minded openness of hand (2 Corinthians 8:2), and repeatedly calls the collection for Jerusalem a charis, a ‘grace’ (2 Corinthians 8:1, 6-7).
ot:
The Bible's account of wealth begins with a world God called good. He places the man in a garden “to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15), and even notes that the gold of Havilah “is pure” (Genesis 2:12). Work, trade, and making things are part of creation, not a result of the fall. The patriarchs are wealthy: Abram “had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold” (Genesis 13:2), and his wealth is presented as God's blessing. Yet Abram refuses the spoils the king of Sodom offers him, “lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich’” (Genesis 14:23), and gives a tenth to Melchizedek, priest of God Most High (Genesis 14:20). Jacob vows a tenth of all God gives him (Genesis 28:22). From the start the question is not whether to have wealth but from whom one receives it and to whom one owes it.

The wilderness gave Israel its first lesson in economics. Each family gathered manna, and “he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall” (Exodus 16:18), while manna hoarded overnight bred maggots. Paul later cites this as the pattern for sharing among the churches (2 Corinthians 8:15). The same people who were given Egypt's gold on their way out melted it into a calf (Exodus 32:2-4), the first of many times the Bible links wealth and idolatry. The Ten Commandments forbid theft and coveting (Exodus 20:15, 17), and the law built limits into the economy: interest-free loans to fellow Israelites in need (Deuteronomy 23:19-20), the release of debts every seventh year, and the Jubilee return of land, because “the land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine” (Leviticus 25:23). Tithes supported the Levites, who had no land (Numbers 18:21), and paid for festive meals before the LORD, and every third year they fed the poor (Deuteronomy 14:22-29). Offering the firstfruits was an act of confession that the land was God's gift, followed by a feast shared with the Levite and the foreigner (Deuteronomy 26:10-11). Deuteronomy 8 names the danger of prosperity with great precision. When Israel has eaten and is full and its silver and gold multiply, “then your heart will become proud, and you will forget the LORD your God” and say, “The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me.” The answer is memory: “remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:14, 17-18).

The history of the kings tests that warning. The king was not to “accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold” (Deuteronomy 17:17). Solomon asked for wisdom rather than riches and was given riches as well (1 Kings 3:11-13), but by the end of his reign gold poured in by the hundreds of talents a year (1 Kings 10:14), and in old age “his wives turned his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4). His son's refusal to lighten the heavy labor Solomon had imposed split the kingdom (1 Kings 12). Ahab's seizure of Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21) shows royal greed trampling the inherited land the law protected; Naboth refused to sell “the inheritance of my fathers” (1 Kings 21:3). At the other end of the story David's prayer at the gathering of gifts for the temple sets out the whole theology of giving: “everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

The wisdom books hold both registers. Proverbs teaches that “diligent hands bring wealth” (Proverbs 10:4) and that “the blessing of the LORD enriches” (Proverbs 10:22), but also that “dishonest wealth will dwindle” (Proverbs 13:11), that “a good name is more desirable than great riches” (Proverbs 22:1), and that wealth “makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky” (Proverbs 23:5). Agur prays, “Give me neither poverty nor riches”, since too much may lead him to deny God and too little to steal (Proverbs 30:8-9). Job, stripped of everything, says, “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21), and he counts trusting in gold as a form of idolatry, a denial of “God on high” (Job 31:24-28). Psalm 49 reminds the envious that the rich man “will carry nothing away” at death (Psalm 49:17), and Psalm 62 warns, “If your riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Psalm 62:10). Ecclesiastes observes that “he who loves money is never satisfied by money” (Ecclesiastes 5:10) and yet calls the ability to enjoy one's wealth “a gift from God” (Ecclesiastes 5:19).

The prophets attack wealth gained by injustice and enjoyed without grief. Isaiah pronounces woe on those “who add house to house and join field to field” until the small farmer is gone (Isaiah 5:8). Amos describes the rich of Samaria lying on ivory beds and drinking wine by the bowlful while they “fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph” (Amos 6:4-6). Hosea says Israel took the silver and gold God gave her and “crafted for Baal” (Hosea 2:8), and Jeremiah forbids the wealthy to boast in their riches rather than in knowing the God who delights in “loving devotion, justice and righteousness” (Jeremiah 9:23-24). After the exile Haggai tells the returned community that their wages go “into a bag pierced through” while God's house lies in ruins (Haggai 1:6), and reminds them, “The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine” (Haggai 2:8). Malachi accuses Judah of robbing God “in tithes and offerings” and summons them to bring the full tithe into the storehouse (Malachi 3:8-10). The Old Testament closes still holding both truths: wealth is God's to give, and it is his to demand back.
nt:
Jesus was born into a poor household and during his ministry said, “the Son of Man has no place to lay His head” (Matthew 8:20). He and his disciples were supported by women who ministered to them “out of their own means” (Luke 8:3), and they kept a common purse, which Judas stole from (John 12:6). Jesus' teaching on possessions is extensive and sharp. In the Sermon on the Mount he tells his hearers not to store up treasure on earth, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21), and he names wealth as a rival master: “You cannot serve both God and money” (Matthew 6:24). He then turns to anxiety, the poor person's temptation as greed is the rich person's, and gives one answer to both: “seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you” (Matthew 6:33). In the parable of the sower, “the deceitfulness of wealth” chokes the word (Matthew 13:22), while in the twin parables of the hidden treasure and the pearl a man sells everything with joy because he has found something worth more (Matthew 13:44-46).

Several encounters show how differently the same demand can land. A rich man asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus, who “looked at him, loved him”, tells him, “Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me” (Mark 10:21). He goes away grieving, and Jesus says, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Mark 10:25). The later explanation that the needle's eye was a small gate in Jerusalem has no ancient evidence behind it; the saying is about impossibility, and Jesus' answer to the astonished disciples is that “all things are possible with God” (Mark 10:27). When a man asks Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute, he refuses and warns instead, “Guard yourselves against every form of greed, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions”, then tells of a rich farmer who builds bigger barns and dies that night, “not rich toward God” (Luke 12:15-21). Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, is not told to sell everything, but gives half to the poor and repays fourfold whatever he has taken by fraud, and Jesus says, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9). A poor widow puts two small coins in the temple treasury, and Jesus says she has given more than the rich, because she gave “all she had to live on” (Luke 21:4). In the difficult parable of the shrewd manager, Jesus tells his disciples to use “worldly wealth” to make friends who will welcome them into eternal dwellings, and he makes faithfulness with money a test of faithfulness with “true riches” (Luke 16:9-11). Luke adds that the Pharisees, “lovers of money”, scoffed (Luke 16:14). And when Jesus drove the traders from the temple courts, he charged that a house of prayer for all nations had become “a den of robbers” (Mark 11:17).

The early church lived out this teaching in more than one way. In Jerusalem believers sold property and shared the proceeds so that no one was in need (Acts 2:44-45; 4:32-35), yet Peter tells Ananias that his land remained his own and the money “at your disposal” (Acts 5:4); his sin was lying to the Holy Spirit, not keeping property. Peter rebukes Simon for thinking “you could buy the gift of God with money” (Acts 8:20). Paul worked with his own hands so as not to burden the churches and quotes a saying of Jesus found nowhere in the Gospels, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). He tells idle believers that anyone “unwilling to work” should not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10) and former thieves to work so they can share with the needy (Ephesians 4:28). His great teaching on giving comes in the collection for Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8 and 9). The Macedonians, in “deep poverty”, overflowed “into rich generosity” because “they gave themselves first to the Lord” (2 Corinthians 8:2, 5). Giving is to be regular and proportionate (1 Corinthians 16:2), free and glad: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). The model is Christ, who “though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

The apostles also warn. Greed is “idolatry” (Colossians 3:5; Ephesians 5:5). Church leaders must be free of the love of money (1 Timothy 3:3), and some treat “godliness as a means of gain” (1 Timothy 6:5). Paul answers that “godliness with contentment is great gain”, that “we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it”, and that “the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:6-10). Yet he does not tell the rich to stop being rich; he tells them not to hope in “the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy”, and to be “generous and ready to share” (1 Timothy 6:17-18). Paul himself had “learned to be content regardless of my circumstances” (Philippians 4:11). Hebrews grounds contentment in God's promise, “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). James warns merchants who plan profits without reckoning with God (James 4:13-14) and landowners whose hoarded riches “have rotted” while their laborers' unpaid wages cry out (James 5:1-5). In Revelation the church at Laodicea says, “I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing”, and is told it is poor, blind, and naked (Revelation 3:17). Babylon, the great trading city, falls, and her merchants' cargo list ends with “slaves and souls of men” (Revelation 18:13). Yet the Bible's last city is built of “pure gold, as clear as glass” (Revelation 21:18), and “the glory and honor of the nations” are brought into it (Revelation 21:26). Wealth is not destroyed in the end but freed from idolatry and brought to the feet of God.

keyTexts.why: Abram gives a tenth to Melchizedek and refuses the king of Sodom's spoils, so that no one but God can say he made Abram rich.
The manna teaches daily dependence: enough for each, no excess for the greedy, and rot for what is hoarded. Paul cites it as the pattern for sharing.
Prosperity breeds forgetfulness and pride. Israel must remember that God gives the power to gain wealth.
David's prayer at the temple offering confesses that everything belongs to God and that giving returns to him what came from his hand.
Trusting in gold is named as a secret idolatry, a denial of God on high, placed beside the worship of sun and moon.
Agur's prayer for neither poverty nor riches names the spiritual danger at both ends of the scale.
The love of money never satisfies and everyone leaves the world naked, yet the power to enjoy one's wealth is a gift of God.
Withholding tithes is robbing God. The passage is central to debates about tithing today.
Treasure and heart, the two masters, and freedom from anxiety through seeking God's kingdom first.
The rich man who cannot let go, the camel and the needle, and the promise that what is impossible for man is possible with God.
Life does not consist in possessions. The rich fool builds bigger barns and dies not rich toward God.
Money is to be used for eternal purposes, faithfulness with little tests faithfulness with much, and no one can serve God and money.
Generosity as grace, modeled on Christ who became poor, and aimed at equality among the churches.
Contentment, the love of money as a root of evils, and a charge to the rich to hope in God and be generous.
Hoarded wealth rots and withheld wages cry out to the Lord of Hosts. The rich are called to account.

history:
The early church received Jesus' teaching on wealth as a real demand and argued over what it required. Around 200 Clement of Alexandria wrote Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, arguing that Jesus' command to the rich man concerns the soul's attachment to wealth rather than the mere fact of owning it, and that a rich Christian can be saved by using wealth well. Others heard the command more literally. Athanasius's Life of Antony (about 360) tells how the young Antony heard Matthew 19:21 read in church, gave away his inheritance, and went into the desert, and his example helped launch the monastic movement, which made voluntary poverty one of its vows. In the fourth century Basil of Caesarea, in a sermon on the rich fool's barns, and John Chrysostom, in sermons on the rich man and Lazarus, argued that surplus kept back from the hungry belongs to the poor. The Council of Nicaea (325), in its seventeenth canon, forbade clergy to lend at interest, and the medieval church extended the ban on usury to all Christians; Thomas Aquinas treated usury as a sin in the Summa Theologiae (II-II, question 78). Francis of Assisi (died 1226) embraced radical poverty, and his followers' claim that Christ and the apostles owned nothing at all, individually or in common, was condemned as heretical by Pope John XXII in the bull Cum inter nonnullos (1323).

The Reformers rejected the idea that renouncing property was a higher way than faithful work and generosity in an ordinary calling. Luther preached and wrote against usury and greedy commerce, including his treatise On Trade and Usury (1524). Calvin, in a letter of 1545, argued that the law's ban on interest was a civil rule for Israel, that lending to the poor must be free, and that moderate interest on commercial loans is not forbidden unless it violates justice and love; his view helped reshape Protestant attitudes to credit. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563), expounding the eighth commandment, forbids not only theft but every greedy scheme and misuse of goods, and requires working faithfully so as to be able to give to those in need (Questions 110 and 111). John Wesley's sermon The Use of Money, on Luke 16:9, gave the Methodists three rules: gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can, with the third as the purpose of the first two, and Wesley lived on a modest income while giving away the rest. Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1904 to 1905) argued, to much later debate, that Protestant discipline and thrift helped form modern capitalism.

In the twentieth century two movements sharpened the question. Prosperity teaching, which grew especially in North American Pentecostal and charismatic circles after the Second World War and spread worldwide, taught that God wills financial wealth for the faithful and that giving is a seed that will return a harvest. A working group of the evangelical Lausanne Movement, meeting at Akropong, Ghana, in 2008 and 2009, judged the teaching of its most vigorous promoters false and gravely distorting of the Bible while granting that some of its themes have biblical roots. Meanwhile Christians argued over wealth and global poverty. Ronald Sider's Rich Christians in an Age of Hunger (1977) called believers in wealthy nations to simpler living and structural change, and Michael Novak's The Spirit of Democratic Capitalism (1982) defended market economies as the greatest engine for lifting people out of poverty. Craig Blomberg's Neither Poverty nor Riches (1999), a biblical theology of possessions, took its title from Agur's prayer.

differ.view: The tithe as a standing standard
differ.body: Many Christians hold that giving a tenth of income to God through the local church remains the normal baseline for believers. They note that tithing appears before the law of Moses (Genesis 14:20; 28:22), that Jesus affirmed the Pharisees' tithing while rebuking their neglect of justice, saying they should have done the one “without neglecting the former” (Matthew 23:23), and that Malachi's call to bring the full tithe expresses a lasting principle of honoring God first. Defenders add that a clear standard protects believers from self-deception about their generosity and teaches them to give first rather than from what is left over, and that grace under the new covenant should lead to more than a tenth, not less.

differ.view: Grace giving without a fixed percentage
differ.body: Others hold that the tithe belonged to Israel's covenant economy, where it supported the Levites, the temple, festivals, and the poor, and that the New Testament never commands Christians to tithe. Paul's teaching on giving asks for regular, proportionate, voluntary, and cheerful giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:7) and points to the Macedonians who gave beyond their means. Defenders argue that a fixed percentage can become a ceiling for the wealthy and a crushing burden for the poor, and that the new covenant asks for the whole life, with generosity measured by Christ's own self-giving rather than by a rule.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians, and some Protestants, hold that Jesus' command to the rich man to sell everything and follow him is, for some believers, a particular calling to be taken literally, embodied in the vow of poverty in monastic and religious life. On this view voluntary poverty is a witness to the whole church that God is enough and that the kingdom is worth everything (Matthew 13:44-46; Mark 10:28-30). Defenders do not claim that all must renounce property or that renouncing it earns salvation; they say that the church needs some who give up everything so that all remember what possessions are for.

The Reformation traditions hold that the ordinary Christian who works, owns, saves, and gives in a secular calling serves God as truly as any monk, and that the Bible's warnings target the love of money and trust in riches rather than ownership as such (1 Timothy 6:10, 17-19). They point to Abraham, Job, Joseph of Arimathea, and the women who supported Jesus out of their means, and to Peter's statement that Ananias's property was his own (Acts 5:4). Defenders see the command to the rich man as a diagnosis of his particular idol, and argue that faithful, generous stewardship spread across a whole congregation does more good than renunciation by a few.

Christians who agree on generosity still differ on economics. Some, like Ronald Sider, stress the Bible's warnings against accumulation and its structures of release, and argue that believers in wealthy nations should live more simply and press for fairer trade and aid. Others, like Michael Novak and, later, Wayne Grudem and Barry Asmus in The Poverty of Nations (2013), stress the Bible's affirmation of work, property, and honest exchange, and argue that the rule of law, free markets, and wealth creation have done more to reduce poverty than redistribution. Both sides appeal to the same texts, the prophets on justice and Proverbs on diligence, and both claim to be serving the poor.

errors:
The church has rejected the prosperity teaching that God promises financial wealth to all who have enough faith or give enough seed money. It turns the Bible's warnings against the love of money into a program for acquiring it, treats God as a means of gain (1 Timothy 6:5), and implies that the poor are faithless, which the poverty of Jesus and his apostles refutes (1 Corinthians 4:11). It has equally rejected the opposite error that material things are evil in themselves or that owning property is sin, a view with roots in ancient teachings that despised the body and the physical world. Creation is good, the Word became flesh, and the new creation is a city of gold.

Other distortions are subtler and more common. One treats giving as a way to buy God's favor or silence conscience while the heart stays attached, which Jesus exposed in the Pharisees and the prophets exposed in Israel's worship. Another assumes that wealth is always earned and poverty always deserved, forgetting that Proverbs also speaks of wealth gained by fraud and of the poor crushed at the gate. A third privatizes the subject, so that money becomes the one area of life a church never speaks about, though Jesus spoke about it often and plainly.
life:
The Bible does not hand the believer a budget. It hands them a question, the one Jesus asked: where is your treasure? It invites people to receive what they have as gifts, to enjoy them with thanks, to work honestly, to pay what they owe, to refuse any gain that comes by exploiting others, and to give generously, regularly, and gladly. It calls them to watch for the signs of money's rule in their own lives, such as anxiety, envy, an inability to give, or a sense that life consists in having more, and to answer them not with guilt but with the promise that God will never leave them.

Contentment is the fruit the New Testament looks for. It is not indifference to need or a vow of poverty for everyone, but the freedom Paul described of being able to have much or little because Christ is enough. A person who is free in this way can hold wealth without being held by it, and can give without fear, knowing that the one who became poor for them has made them rich in a way no market can measure.
questions: Deuteronomy 8 warns that prosperity leads to forgetting God. In what concrete ways does comfort make it harder for you or your community to remember where everything comes from?

Jesus told one rich man to sell everything, while Zacchaeus gave half and the women who followed Jesus supported him from their means. What do these different responses suggest about how Jesus' call meets different people?
Paul calls generosity a grace and greed a form of idolatry. What would it look like for giving in your life to be an act of worship rather than an obligation or a way to feel better?
